lead: One short pulse of light entering a multimode fiber leaves stretched. Different modes take different zig-zag paths, so they arrive at different times: the axial ray first, the steepest guided ray last. This is intermodal dispersion, also called modal dispersion. It grows with length L and fractional index difference Δ, and caps the bit rate of a multimode link. Graded-index profiles shrink it by a factor of about 2/Δ — roughly two hundred times at Δ = 0.01 — and a single-mode fiber removes it completely.
prereq: Guided modes, numerical aperture, and the step-versus-graded index profile from Unit 1, Foundations: Light Propagation in Fibers.

blocks.text: A multimode step-index fiber carries many modes. Only the two extremes set the spread. The axial ray runs straight along the core. Its path is the fiber length L, so it arrives at t₁ = L n₁ / c. Here n₁ is the core refractive index (a pure number), L is length in metres, and c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

The steepest guided ray still obeys total internal reflection. At the limiting angle, cos θ = n₂ / n₁, where n₂ is the cladding index. Its zig-zag path is L / cos θ = L n₁ / n₂, and it travels at speed c / n₁. So t₂ = (L n₁ / n₂)(n₁ / c) = L n₁² / (c n₂).
ΔT = t₂ − t₁ = (L n₁ / c) × (n₁ / n₂ − 1) ≈ L n₁ Δ / c
blocks.where: ΔT is the delay difference in seconds; t₁, t₂ are arrival times in seconds; L is length in metres; n₁, n₂ are core and cladding indices; Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁ is the fractional index difference, a pure number of order 0.01; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

blocks.text: The approximation is safe because n₂ is within 1–2 % of n₁. Put in n₁ = 1.48 and Δ = 0.01: ΔT / L = 1.48 × 0.01 / (3 × 10⁸) = 4.93 × 10⁻¹¹ s per metre, about 50 ns per kilometre. A 5 km link smears each pulse by roughly 250 ns, too wide for a 100 ns bit slot.

sections.h3: Graded index: fast rays through slow glass

blocks.text: A graded-index core has highest index on the axis and a smooth fall toward the cladding. Rays far from the axis travel longer paths in lower-index glass, where speed c / n is higher. The longer path is partly cancelled by the higher average speed, so those rays catch up with the axial ray.

blocks.where: ΔT is delay spread in seconds; L is length in metres; n₁ is axial core index; Δ is fractional index difference; c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Valid for the best profile shape, α ≈ 2, where n(r) = n₁[1 − 2Δ(r/a)^α]^(1/2), r is radial distance and a is core radius.

blocks.text: Compare the two results. The ratio is Δ/2, so Δ = 0.01 gives about 200 times improvement. Per kilometre: 1.48 × (0.01)² / (2 × 3 × 10⁸) = 2.47 × 10⁻¹³ s per metre, about 0.25 ns per kilometre instead of 50. The figure plots both lines. This is why graded-index multimode fiber served campus LANs and data centres for years; the cost is a tightly controlled index profile during drawing.

sections.h3: Bit rate limit, RMS width, and adding spreads

blocks.text: A bit slot must be longer than the spread, or pulse 1 spills into slot 2. The working rule below uses factor 2 as a safety margin. Because ΔT grows with L, B·L is roughly constant for a fiber type — the bandwidth–length product, quoted in MHz·km. Doubling reach halves bit rate.

blocks.where: B is bit rate in bit/s; ΔT is total pulse spread in seconds. Both times — the spread ΔT and the bit period 1/B — must be in the same unit (both ns, or both s) before you compare them.

blocks.text: A real pulse is not rectangular. Engineers quote RMS width σ, the standard deviation in time of its optical power. Independent spreads add in quadrature, never directly.

blocks.where: σ_total, σ_modal, σ_chromatic are RMS pulse widths in seconds; σ_modal is this chapter's intermodal term (about ΔT/√12 for a rectangular pulse); σ_chromatic is the source-spectral-width term, covered in 2.6.

blocks.text: A single-mode fiber guides only one mode, so σ_modal = 0 and no intermodal term exists. That is why single-mode fiber wins on long haul. Unit 5, Link Design and Fiber Measurements, combines all terms into the rise-time budget.

figure.caption: Pulse spread against length at Δ = 0.01 for the two profiles: about 50 ns per kilometre for step index and 0.25 ns per kilometre for graded index. At 10 km the graded line has reached only 2.5 ns while the step-index line is at 500 ns.

spec.aria: Two straight lines of pulse spread against length: the step-index line climbs two hundred times faster than the graded-index line.

examples.question: A step-index multimode fiber has core index n₁ = 1.48, fractional index difference Δ = 0.01 and length L = 5 km. (a) Find the intermodal delay difference ΔT. (b) Estimate the maximum bit rate using B ≤ 1/(2ΔT). (c) Repeat both parts for a graded-index fiber with the optimum near-parabolic profile.
steps: Use SI units: L = 5000 m, n₁ = 1.48, Δ = 0.01, c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
Axial transit time: L n₁ / c = (5000 × 1.48) / (3 × 10⁸) = 2.467 × 10⁻⁵ s.
(c) B ≤ 1 / (2 × 1.233 × 10⁻⁹) = 4.054 × 10⁸ bit/s ≈ 405 Mbit/s, about 200 times the step-index figure.
examples.answer: Step index: ΔT ≈ 247 ns and B ≈ 2.0 Mbit/s. Optimum graded index: ΔT ≈ 1.23 ns and B ≈ 405 Mbit/s.
examples.check:
n1 = 1.48
Delta = 0.01
L = 5000.0
c = 3e8
dT_step = L * n1 * Delta / c
print(round(dT_step * 1e9, 2))
print(round((1 / (2 * dT_step)) / 1e6, 3))
dT_grad = L * n1 * Delta**2 / (2 * c)
print(round(dT_grad * 1e9, 3))
print(round((1 / (2 * dT_grad)) / 1e6, 1))

traps: Using Δ = n₁ − n₂ instead of Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁. For n₁ = 1.48 and n₂ = 1.465, Δ is 0.01, not 0.015.
Losing units. A spread in seconds and a bit period in nanoseconds must be converted to the same unit before comparison.
Adding spreads directly, σ_total = σ_modal + σ_chromatic. Independent mechanisms add in quadrature, so the true total is smaller.
Expecting intermodal dispersion in a single-mode fiber. With one mode there is no path-difference term; any spread is chromatic (2.6) or polarization mode (2.7).
Writing B = 1/ΔT and forgetting the factor 2 in B ≤ 1/(2ΔT), which doubles the claimed bit rate. Also, B·L is roughly constant for a fiber type, so bandwidth without a length means nothing.

quiz.q: Define intermodal dispersion and state where it occurs.
quiz.a: It is pulse spreading because different guided modes travel different path lengths and arrive at different times. It occurs only in multimode fiber; a single-mode fiber has one mode and one path delay.

quiz.q: Why does a graded-index profile reduce intermodal dispersion?
quiz.a: The index falls with radius. A ray far from the axis travels a longer path but spends most of it in lower-index glass, where speed c/n is higher. The speed gain partly cancels the path excess, so high-order rays catch up with the axial ray.

quiz.q: Why is the intermodal spread proportional to Δ for a step-index fiber but to Δ² for an optimum graded-index fiber?
quiz.a: In a step index the core index is uniform, so spread comes only from path length, which varies as Δ. In a graded index the speed gain at radius r is itself proportional to the local index deficit, of order Δ. Path excess and speed gain both scale with Δ, so residual spread scales as Δ².

quiz.q: A step-index multimode fiber has n₁ = 1.5, Δ = 0.02 and L = 2 km. Find ΔT and the maximum bit rate.
Repeat the previous question for an optimum graded-index fiber with the same n₁, Δ and length.
quiz.a: ΔT = (L n₁/c) × Δ²/2 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ × (4 × 10⁻⁴)/2 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁹ s = 2 ns. B ≤ 1/(2 × 2.0 × 10⁻⁹) = 2.5 × 10⁸ bit/s = 250 Mbit/s, a hundred times better because the ratio is Δ/2 = 0.01.

quiz.q: A 3 km link must carry 100 Mbit/s. Using 50 ns/km for step index and 0.25 ns/km for graded index at Δ = 0.01, decide which multimode fiber can do the job.
quiz.a: Allowed spread: ΔT ≤ 1/(2B) = 1/(2 × 100 × 10⁶) = 5 ns. Step index gives 50 × 3 = 150 ns, too large; its limit is about 3.3 Mbit/s. Graded index gives 0.25 × 3 = 0.75 ns, limit about 667 Mbit/s. Only the graded-index fiber works at 3 km.

beyond: Not for the exam. Laser-optimized multimode fiber (OM3, OM4, OM5) is drawn for low spread at 850 nm and driven by VCSELs in data centres over a few hundred metres. In few-mode fiber, intermodal spread becomes a fixed channel property that digital signal processing equalizes; MIMO receivers untangle the modes. Multicore fiber gives each core its own path, so modes in different cores never mix.
